findings.title: Async forEach callback makes the surrounding try/catch dead and leaves calendar cancellations unawaited
findings.body: The callback passed to bookingRefsFiltered.forEach is now async and awaits getCalendar(). forEach ignores the promises its callback returns, so the try/catch at lines 124-139 can no longer catch anything. Before this change, a synchronous throw from getCalendar (for example a CalendarService constructor error) was caught and logged. Now every throw becomes a rejected promise nobody handles, so it surfaces as an unhandledRejection and the logger.error branch never runs. The function also returns true at line 151 before the calendar and video cancellations have run. The identical change in packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts line 125 has the same problem. Use a for...of loop with await inside the try so failures are caught and ordering is preserved.

findings.title: requestReschedule fires async callbacks through forEach with no awaiting or error handling
findings.body: The forEach callback is now async and awaits getCalendar() before calendar.deleteEvent(). forEach does not await these promises, so the mutation finishes and responds while calendar and video cancellations may still be in flight. Any failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Before this change, a synchronous throw from getCalendar would propagate out of the mutation and fail it visibly; now that error is silently swallowed as an unhandled rejection. Use for...of with await, or Promise.allSettled with explicit logging, so the outcome of the cancellations is observed.

findings.title: Recurring-cancel calendar deletions are no longer awaited before the response
findings.body: The outer .forEach(async (credential) => {...}) pushes deletion results into apiDeletes from inside an async callback that nothing awaits. apiDeletes is snapshotted by prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes) in the later Promise.all, so these pushes arrive too late to be awaited, and their errors are unhandled. This PR adds another await before deleteEvent is called, so the calendar deletions are now issued a microtask later, after the handler has already moved on toward the response. The same PR converts the non-recurring 'old behaviour' branch just below to a for...of loop with await (lines 477-484), so the recurring branch is inconsistent with the intended pattern. On serverless runtimes, work still pending after the response can be frozen and never complete. Convert this to for...of with await and push into apiDeletes before the Promise.all.

findings.title: Import failure in getVideoAdapters escapes the Cal Video fallback in createMeeting
findings.body: getVideoAdapters now awaits a dynamic import from appStore. Line 52 calls it outside the try block that starts at line 70, and the catch at line 86 is where createMeeting falls back to Cal Video. If the dynamic import rejects (module evaluation error, missing dependency, or a chunk load failure), createMeeting rejects immediately instead of falling back, so the whole booking or reschedule that uses the video location fails. updateMeeting has the same shape at line 111, where the await is also outside its .catch. Before this change, appStore lookups were synchronous and could not reject. Move the adapter resolution inside the try, or catch the import failure and return the fallback.

findings.title: Eagerly created import() promises can produce unhandled rejections
findings.body: Each entry in the appStore object is an import() promise created at module evaluation. Only the keys that a caller actually awaits get a rejection handler. If any app module throws while evaluating, its promise rejects and nothing handles it, which Node reports as an unhandledRejection (process termination under default settings on modern Node). With the previous static imports, the same failure surfaced deterministically at startup. Consider storing factories (() => import(...)) and awaiting only the requested app, or attaching a handler to each promise.

findings.title: import() in an object literal still loads every app eagerly
findings.body: The object literal calls import() for all 28 apps as soon as the module is evaluated, so every app module still loads at startup, just asynchronously. The PR does not make app loading lazy, and the extra awaits at every call site add complexity without a corresponding saving. If the goal is lazy loading, the entries need to be functions such as () => import('./vital') that are invoked only when needed.

findings.title: Default export values changed from modules to Promises; unconverted callers fail silently
findings.body: appStore's values changed from module namespaces to Promise<module>. Any call site that still indexes appStore synchronously, including code outside the 12 changed files, now receives a Promise. The guard pattern used throughout, `if (!(app && 'lib' in app && 'CalendarService' in app.lib))`, evaluates `'lib' in promise` as false and takes the 'not implemented' branch, returning null with only a warning. Calendar events, video meetings, or payments would then be skipped silently rather than erroring. TypeScript does not flag this because `in` accepts any object type. Every consumer of the default export needs to be checked for a missing await.

findings.title: Commented-out example import points at a path that does not exist
findings.body: The old file used `// import * as example from "./_example";`. The new comment refers to `import("./example")`, which drops the leading underscore and so points to the wrong module if someone uncomments it.

findings.title: getCalendarCredentials returns an unawaited Promise in the calendar field
findings.body: getCalendarCredentials stays synchronous, but getCalendar is now async, so each returned entry's `calendar` field is a Promise<Calendar | null> that is never awaited here. The exported return shape changed silently. Callers that read `.calendar` as a Calendar would fail type-checking, and any rejection (for example an import failure) is unhandled if the entry is never consumed. Making this function async and awaiting each calendar, or documenting the Promise field, would make the contract explicit.
